title: ⭐ Practice: the map, the ad and the vowel

questions.prompt: Sami's cousin was born in Cardiff. Complete what a geography teacher would say about her birthplace: it is …

options.text: in the United Kingdom, but not on the island of Great Britain
in the United Kingdom and on the island of Great Britain as well
on the island of Great Britain, but outside the United Kingdom
neither in the United Kingdom nor on the island of Great Britain

questions.explanation: Cardiff is the capital of Wales, and Wales is doubly inside: it is one of the four constituent countries of the United Kingdom, and it shares the island of Great Britain with England and Scotland. Two of the other three descriptions fit real places, and finding them yourself is the exercise: one is true of every town in the corner of Ireland that belongs to the United Kingdom, the other of every town in the independent republic beside it. The third fits nothing on earth — no birthplace can stand on Great Britain and yet outside the United Kingdom, because every square metre of that island lies inside the state.

questions.prompt:
Here is a whole ad, printed on a board outside a station:

EDINBURGH ON FOOT — THE OLD TOWN WALK
Every morning at 10.30 · Leaves from the fountain in Princes Street
Two hours of easy walking · No booking needed · Adults £12
The castle esplanade, the closes, the Grassmarket

A visitor reads it twice and still cannot answer one of these four questions. Which one?

options.text: Must I reserve a place, or may I simply turn up on the day?
How much of my morning must I keep free for this walk?
Which exact spot in the city does the group leave from, and when?
Where in the city will I be standing when the walk is over?

questions.explanation: The ad prints where the walk leaves from and never prints where it leaves you: no booking is needed and the board says so in as many words, the group gathers at the fountain in Princes Street at half past ten, and the two hours are printed on the third line — but the finishing point is nowhere on the board. That silence is normal, and it is deliberate: an ad prints what brings you and leaves out what might put you off, and a walk that ends a mile from your hotel is exactly the kind of thing that puts a reader off. Reading an ad well means reading it twice, once for what it says and once for what it has quietly left out.

questions.prompt: A guide is proof-reading four captions for the town's website. One of them says two things that cannot both be true. Which caption must he rewrite?

options.text: Edinburgh is a cosmopolitan city: you hear five languages in one street.
The old harbour is a busy venue: three concerts are held there each week.
The botanical garden is open year round, so it shuts from October to March.
Scotland shares a land border with England: you can walk from one to the other.

questions.explanation: Year round means every season of the year without a break — so a garden that is open year round cannot shut for six months of it. The caption puts a fact and its own contradiction in the same breath, and only the meaning of the words catches it: no rule of grammar is broken. The other three hold together perfectly. A cosmopolitan city is one where a dozen nationalities live side by side, and five languages in one street is the proof. A venue is a place where shows are held, so three concerts a week is what a busy one looks like. And a land border is one you can cross on foot, which is exactly what Scotland and England share.

questions.prompt: A pronunciation drill sorts words by the vowel in their stressed syllable. Match each key word of the lesson with the travel word that carries the SAME vowel sound.

options.text: walk
first
guard
odd
market
shop
autumn
return

questions.explanation: Read the letters as a group and the four sounds fall into place. Walk and autumn share the long /ɔː/, spelt al in one and au in the other — the vowel of north and more. First and return share the long /ɜː/, spelt ir and ur, the vowel of church and world. Guard and market share the long /ɑː/ that the letters ar almost always give, as in park and star. And odd and shop share the short /ɒ/ of a single o shut in by consonants, as in novel and stop. Three of the four are long and one is short, which is the whole point of the drill: the two dots in the symbol tell you to hold the sound.

questions.prompt: A tourist office has this true sentence on its website: "The walk leaves Trafalgar Square at ten every morning and lasts two hours." The office now wants a line that PERSUADES rather than one that informs. Which line does that job?

options.text: Be at Trafalgar Square at ten and give us two fine hours of your holiday.
The walk sets off from Trafalgar Square at ten and is over again by midday.
In my opinion these two hours are the finest way of seeing the city.
Visitors have been setting off from Trafalgar Square at ten since 1998.

questions.explanation: Persuading turns the sentence towards the reader. An imperative gives him something to do — be there at ten — and the rest of the line tells him what he gets out of it, two fine hours of his own holiday. That is the whole recipe: you, an action, a benefit. Setting off again by midday only re-words the timetable, so it still informs and nothing more. Starting with in my opinion hands the sentence an owner: it says what the writer thinks, not what the reader should do, and an opinion — superlative or no superlative — persuades nobody who has not already asked for it. And giving the year 1998 only adds one more checkable fact to the same notice: it informs a second time, and a reader who was not going to come is no nearer coming.

questions.prompt: A guidebook prints: "Aberdeen is the third largest city in Scotland." How many Scottish cities are larger than Aberdeen?

options.text: Three cities are larger, since Aberdeen comes after them.
Two cities are larger — the ones ranked first and second.
One city only is larger, the one at the very top of the list.
Nobody can tell: the number is not given by the sentence.

questions.explanation: An ordinal number in front of a superlative counts the places above, and it counts them exactly: third largest means two cities are larger and Aberdeen comes next. The trap is to read the ordinal as if it counted the cities that are larger — third does not mean three above, it means Aberdeen holds the third position. And the sentence is far from silent on the number: that is precisely what the word third has been put there to say. The same machinery runs the whole family — the second largest city has exactly one above it, the largest city has none.
